title: Evaluating models
summary: A score is a procedure, not a fact. Perplexity is exp of the mean negative log-likelihood and only compares models with the same tokenizer. Multiple-choice benchmarks are often scored by option likelihood, where length normalisation matters. Code uses pass@k with an unbiased estimator. Every score has a standard error, benchmarks can leak into training data, and LLM judges have position, length and self-preference biases.
llm_link: Your own evals for RAG and agents face the same issues: define the scoring procedure exactly, report uncertainty (a 1-point gain on 200 questions is usually noise), keep test items out of prompts and fine-tuning data, and swap answer order when an LLM judges two outputs.
key_ideas: Perplexity = exp(−(1/N)·Σ log p(true token)). A uniform guess over k tokens has perplexity k. Not comparable across tokenizers.

Multiple choice by likelihood: score each option's log-probability given the question; sum vs. per-token mean (length normalisation) can change the pick. GPT-3 used per-token normalisation for most tasks.
pass@k (Chen et al., 2021): draw n samples, c pass; unbiased estimate 1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k).
Standard error of an accuracy p on n items ≈ √(p(1−p)/n): about 2 points at 70% on 500 questions.
Contamination: test items seen in pretraining inflate scores; check overlap, use private or fresh test sets.
LLM-as-judge (Zheng et al., 2023, MT-Bench): GPT-4 agreement with humans was similar to human-human agreement, with position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases. Swap order and average.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a model gives every true token probability 0.25. What is its perplexity?
quiz.explain: exp(−log 0.25) = 1/0.25 = 4: as uncertain as a fair choice among 4 tokens.

quiz.q: Model A scores 71% and model B 70% on 500 questions. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: The gap is within about one standard error (≈2 points), so it may be noise
B is better because scores are noisy
quiz.explain: √(0.7·0.3/500) ≈ 0.02. A 1-point difference is well inside that, so more questions or a paired comparison is needed.

quiz.q: Why can't you compare the perplexity of two models with different tokenizers directly?
options: Perplexity is always 1 for large models
The averages are over different units (tokens), so the models are scored on different prediction tasks
quiz.explain: A tokenizer that splits text into more, smaller pieces makes each prediction easier but requires more of them. Compare per-character or per-byte measures instead.

quiz.q: A coding model passes the tests on 3 of 10 samples for a problem. What is the unbiased pass@1 estimate?
quiz.explain: For k = 1 the formula 1 − C(7,1)/C(10,1) = 1 − 7/10 = 0.3, the fraction of samples that pass.

quiz.q: You ask an LLM judge which of two RAG answers is better, always listing your new system's answer first. What bias should you guard against?
options: Position bias: judges can favour the answer shown first; swap the order and average
quiz.explain: MT-Bench documented position bias. Running both orders and keeping only consistent verdicts (or averaging) removes most of it.

problems.title: Perplexity
problems.prompt:
Write perplexity(probs): probs is a list of the probabilities the model gave to each true next token in a held-out text. Return exp(-(1/N) · Σ log p).

perplexity([0.25, 0.25, 0.25])   # 4.0
perplexity([0.5, 0.125])          # 4.0 (geometric mean of 1/p)

tests.name: uniform over four
tests.code:
out = perplexity([0.25, 0.25, 0.25])
assert out is not None, 'perplexity returned None'
assert abs(out - 4.0) < 1e-9, f'a model that gives each true token 1/4 is as unsure as a 4-way guess: expected 4.0, got {out}'

tests.name: geometric, not arithmetic
tests.code:
out = perplexity([0.5, 0.125])
assert abs(out - 4.0) < 1e-9, f'expected exp(-(log 0.5 + log 0.125)/2) = 4.0, got {out}. If you got 3.2 you averaged probabilities instead of log-probabilities.'

tests.name: perfect model
tests.code:
out = perplexity([1.0, 1.0])
assert abs(out - 1.0) < 1e-12, f'certainty on every true token gives perplexity 1, got {out}'

tests.name: worse predictions, higher perplexity
tests.code: assert perplexity([0.1, 0.1]) > perplexity([0.5, 0.5]), 'lower probabilities on the true tokens must give higher perplexity'

hints: nll = -sum(math.log(p) for p in probs) / len(probs)

problems.title: Unbiased pass@k
problems.prompt:
For one problem you drew n programs and c of them passed the tests. Write pass_at_k(n, c, k) = 1 − C(n−c, k) / C(n, k), where C is "n choose k" (math.comb).

When there are fewer than k failing samples (n − c < k), every choice of k includes a pass, so return 1.0.

pass_at_k(10, 3, 1)   # 0.3
pass_at_k(10, 3, 5)   # 0.9166...
problems.starter:

def pass_at_k(n, c, k):

    # TODO 2: 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)
    pass

tests.name: k = 1 is the pass rate
tests.code:
out = pass_at_k(10, 3, 1)
assert out is not None and abs(out - 0.3) < 1e-12, f'pass@1 should equal c/n = 0.3, got {out}'

tests.name: no passes
tests.code: assert pass_at_k(20, 0, 5) == 0.0, 'if no sample passes, pass@k must be 0'

tests.name: too few failures
tests.code:
out = pass_at_k(5, 3, 3)
assert out == 1.0, f'with only 2 failing samples, any 3 chosen include a pass: expected 1.0, got {out}'

tests.name: grows with k
tests.code:
vals = [pass_at_k(50, 5, k) for k in (1, 5, 10)]
assert vals[0] < vals[1] < vals[2], f'more attempts can only help: got {vals}'

hints:
if n - c < k: return 1.0
return 1 - math.comb(n - c, k) / math.comb(n, k)

problems.title: Scoring multiple choice by likelihood
problems.prompt:
For a question, each answer option has a list of per-token log-probabilities (the model's log-prob of each token of that option, given the question). Write pick(option_logprobs, normalize) that returns the index of the chosen option:

  • normalize=False: highest sum of log-probs
  • normalize=True: highest mean log-prob per token
opts = [[-1.0], [-0.4, -0.4, -0.4]]
pick(opts, False)   # 0  (sum -1.0 beats -1.2)
pick(opts, True)    # 1  (mean -0.4 beats -1.0)

The same model, the same question, two different "answers": this is why an evaluation must state how it scores.

assert out == 1, f'means are -1.0 and -0.4, so option 1 wins; got {out}'
